title: Which Assets Will Benefit from the El Niño Phenomenon?
summary: According to market sources, the probability of El Niño in 2026 exceeds 82%, with potential for an extreme tail risk. Sugar prices are at a six-year cycle bottom, palm oil and natural rubber lag behind ONI peak by 4-5 quarters before reaching price highs, cotton is constrained by demand and inventory, and thermal power coal faces a summer electricity window - but the 2023 example has shown that weather-driven gains do not necessarily translate into price gains. Whether production cuts can penetrate inventory and trade channels is the real deciding factor.
content:
The weather variable in 2026 is no longer just meteorological news. The National Climate Center's April monitoring estimates that 2026 May will enter an El Niño state and form a moderate or stronger El Niño event during the summer and autumn, lasting at least until the end of this year. NOAA's May forecast also shows a high probability: the likelihood of El Niño occurring between May and July 2026 is over 82%, with a 96% chance of continuing through the Northern Hemisphere winter, and a probability of exceeding 30% of developing into an extreme category in November.

Analysts from Guosheng Securities, including Xu Wenhui, pointed out in their report on May 20 that 'The 2026 El Niño event will cause climatic disturbances in major agricultural producing areas such as sugar, palm oil, rubber, and cotton, potentially driving reduced production and thus pushing up prices.' This same climatic chain will also affect summer electricity demand in China: northern drought and southern flooding, rising temperatures, may increase thermal power generation and demand for power coal.

The most notable point is not simply 'El Niño comes, commodities rise.' Sugar is also combined with its own approximately six-year price cycle, showing signs of a cycle bottom in 2026; palm oil and natural rubber often do not immediately reach their peaks, but rather see price highs about four quarters after the ONI index peaks, 4-5 quarters later; cotton is more constrained by demand and inventory, and in 2023-2024, prices reached peaks before the ONI index did.

Therefore, historical maximum price increases cannot be directly extrapolated into 2026 returns. What truly needs attention are three things: whether the weather in the main producing areas translates into actual production cuts, whether the production cuts enter the inventory and trade channels, and whether the price response lags and is fulfilled.

The probability of this round of El Niño is not low, and the intensity also has tail risks

The definition of El Niño is not complicated: when the three-month moving average of the NINO3.4 index reaches or exceeds 0.5°C and lasts for at least five months, it can be classified as an El Niño event. According to peak intensity, events with 0.5°C to below 1.3°C are weak, those between 1.3°C to below 2.0°C are moderate, those between 2.0°C to below 2.5°C are strong, and those above 2.5°C are extreme.

Since 1980, there have been 13 El Niño events, including six moderate events and three extreme events. The duration of nine events of moderate or higher intensity ranges from seven to 19 months, mostly peaking during the Northern Hemisphere winter.

The direction of climate impact is relatively clear: Southeast Asia and Australia are more prone to high temperatures and droughts, increasing the risk of forest fires; China is more likely to experience northern drought and southern flooding; South America and the southern part of North America are prone to heavy rain; the central and eastern parts of North America are more prone to high temperatures.

This explains why agricultural products, thermal power, and coal have simultaneously entered the observation list. The former looks at supply disruptions, while the latter looks at summer electricity demand.

Sugar is not purely a weather trade, but also on a six-year cycle

Sugar is the most special type of asset in this review. Global sugar production mainly occurs in Brazil, India, the EU, Thailand, and China, accounting for about 60% of global output. Its price shows a clear six-year complete cycle feature.

In the past three cycles:

  • 2014-2016: About 48%;

title: The 'Impossible Triangle' of the Strait of Hormuz
summary: Global markets are betting on a dangerous 'impossible triangle': financial risk premiums near a 20-year low, oil inventories potentially reaching critical levels in June, and a 30% probability of the Strait of Hormuz reopening. Bank of America Merrill Lynch warns that these three cannot coexist - once inventory buffers are exhausted, demand destruction will trigger an oil price shockwave impacting the global economy, while macroeconomic cracks hidden by the AI boom are widening, and the market's calm may just be a prelude to a storm.
content:
Global markets are simultaneously betting on three conflicting propositions - risk premiums at a 20-year low, oil inventories about to run out, and the strait remaining closed indefinitely. Bank of America Merrill Lynch warns that this 'impossible triangle' means the market severely underestimates the risk of demand destruction.

According to market observers, Bank of America Merrill Lynch strategists Sebastian Raedler and others in a report released on May 22 noted that since the Iranian conflict began in late February, European equities have only fallen 2%, while global equities have risen 4% and reached record highs.

The calm in the market mainly relies on three pillars: relatively moderate increases in oil prices (due to ample prior inventory), resilient U.S. macroeconomic data (supported by early-year large-scale tax refunds), and an AI investment boom driving global earnings momentum far beyond what the macroeconomic fundamentals imply. However, these supports are gradually weakening.

Three Propositions, One Contradiction

The report characterizes the current market pricing as three incompatible propositions, calling it the 'impossible triangle of the Strait of Hormuz.'

The first proposition: financial risk premiums are approaching a 20-year low. The recent rebound in asset prices has compressed financial risk premiums back to near年初's 20-year low. The European equity risk premium (ERP) is currently 4.75%, just 25 basis points above its recent low; the U.S. high-yield credit spread is 275 basis points, only 15 basis points above its recent low. With global growth momentum as the main driver, the current risk premium level implies the market expects global PMI to moderately recover from current levels, rather than being dragged down by energy supply shocks.

The second proposition: oil inventories will fall to critical levels. Given that oil inventories have been significantly depleted, 'it is crucial to quickly restore energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz to prevent a major economic recession.' Several market participants believe that, at the current rate of consumption, global oil inventories may reach operational pressure levels around June. If the inventory buffer is exhausted, supply-demand imbalance will only be adjusted through demand destruction - that is, oil prices will further rise until demand is suppressed, which aligns with historical experiences of energy price shocks.

Some investors believe demand destruction will primarily occur in emerging markets, with the U.S., as a net energy exporter, able to remain unaffected. However, oil is a globally priced commodity, and demand destruction will impact all economies through higher gasoline prices, further depressing U.S. household real income growth.

The third proposition: the market predicts a low probability of the strait reopening in the short term. According to the prediction market platform Kalshi, the probability of the Strait of Hormuz resuming navigation before the end of June has dropped from 75% in mid-April to about 30%, and the probability of resuming before early August is also only 40%.

Different from the previous trade war, this confrontation around the Strait of Hormuz is a multi-party game - both the U.S. and Iran believe waiting for the other side to bear more pain is beneficial for themselves, which could extend the duration of the conflict beyond investors' expectations. The Iranian regime can maintain fiscal operations through limited oil exports and has the capacity to sustain the situation.

The tension between the three propositions is evident: if the strait remains closed as predicted by the market and inventory buffers are depleting, the current pricing of demand destruction risk is overly optimistic.

Macro Resilience Is Fading

Despite the calm in the market, macroeconomic data has shown divergence. In the U.S., labor market, consumer, and capital expenditure data have remained strong so far, but the support effect from the early-year large-scale tax refunds has already faded, and "the true test of consumer and labor market resilience may not have arrived yet." U.S. real labor income growth has fallen to a recession level due to inflation pressures from rising energy prices, and the core PCE inflation in the U.S. is expected to remain slightly above 3% over the next few months.

The situation in the eurozone is even more severe. The eurozone composite PMI new orders index fell to a two-year low of 47.1 in May, and the eurozone private final demand growth is expected to slow significantly over the next few quarters. European natural gas prices have continued to rise since the Iranian conflict began, adding extra pressure on the eurozone PMI.

Notably, global earnings momentum is still significantly exceeding the level implied by macroeconomic fundamentals - the 3-month change in forward earnings per share for the U.S. is 8%, and for Europe, it is 5%, both the strongest since 2021, driven mainly by financial, resource, and technology sectors fueled by the AI investment boom. However, Bank of America Merrill Lynch expects that as macroeconomic pressures take effect, the 12-month forward earnings per share of the Stoxx 600 will decline by about 5% from the current historical high, corresponding to a 2026 earnings growth rate of -1%, below the market's bottom-up consensus forecast.

title: The Contradictory Trends of US Equities and Treasuries: Who Will Win Next?
summary: The divergence between US equities and Treasuries is approaching a critical point. A BCA Research chief strategist warns that the S&P 500's up-and-down line has diverged from the index's movement, with only 55% of its components above the 200-day moving average, indicating that the tech sector's dominance is unsustainable. Rising bond yields, persistently high inflation, and the Federal Reserve's difficult policy choices have created three pressures, suggesting that a substantial market correction may be imminent, with emerging markets likely to be hit first.
content:
US equities and Treasuries are heading toward an unavoidable collision. With persistent inflation and limited monetary policy space, the simultaneous rise in stock prices and bond yields is unsustainable, and the gap between them will eventually be closed by a significant decline in one of them.

Recently, Arthur Budaghyan, chief strategist at BCA Research, released a report stating that the current rally in the US stock market is heavily concentrated in the technology sector, and the internal structure of the market has clearly deteriorated. The sustained increase in bond yields could serve as the trigger for a substantive market correction.

He argues that only a clear decline in the US stock market can lower bond yields and thus release anti-inflationary forces on the economic level. The report also warns that global risk assets, especially emerging markets, will face significant volatility in the coming months.

This implies that the risk-reward ratio of current global risk assets has significantly deteriorated. US equities, emerging market stocks, and high-yield credit bonds all face downward pressure, while the dollar may remain strong in the short term but remains in a weak trend in the medium term.

The Fed Faces a Dilemma, and Bond Market Pressure Remains

The Federal Reserve now faces a difficult decision on whether to raise interest rates, and neither choice will be favorable for the market.

According to a BCA Research report, the yield on the two-year US Treasury note has recently risen above the federal funds rate. Historical data shows that over the past 30 years, whenever the two-year yield crossed above the federal funds rate, the Fed subsequently raised rates. This indicates that expectations for rate hikes have significantly increased.

At the same time, inflation data continues to exceed target levels. Core CPI in the United States is significantly above 2%, and the PPI for final demand (excluding energy and food) has surged to 5.25%, with its six-month annualized change rate reaching 6.6% in April. The report also points out that the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz is unlikely to be resolved in the short term, and oil price upward risks are significant. Oil prices and US Treasury yields have shown a strong correlation this year, further compressing the space for a significant decline in bond yields.

The report emphasizes that even if the new Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh persuades the Federal Open Market Committee to delay raising rates, the Fed's policy statements and inclinations will become significantly more hawkish. More importantly, when inflation rises and the central bank delays action, the market often expects larger future rate hikes, which could lead to further selling in the bond market. "The central bank falling behind the inflation curve is bearish for both stocks and bonds," the report states.

Market Structure Deteriorates, Rally Hides Concerns

title: Dingdong Maicai Awaits Integration into Meituan, Front-End Warehouses Still Contributing Growth
summary: Transition Period Report
content:
Dingdong Maicai released its first financial report after Meituan announced the acquisition of its China business.

In the first quarter, Dingdong Maicai's GMV reached 6.33 billion yuan, up 6.3% year-on-year; total revenue was 5.893 billion yuan, up 7.5% year-on-year; it has achieved consecutive growth in GMV and revenue for the ninth quarter in a row.

During the reporting period, Dingdong Maicai's total net profit was 165 million yuan, and its Non-GAAP net profit was 172 million yuan.

However, due to the accounting treatment related to Meituan transactions, the company classified long-term assets related to its China business as assets held for sale and ceased depreciation and amortization, which increased net profit by approximately 138 million yuan.

Excluding this impact, the actual operating net profit was approximately 28 million yuan, a 2.4-fold increase compared to 80 million yuan in the same period last year.

This financial report therefore carries a special transitional character. Currently, the transaction where Meituan acquired Dingdong Maicai's China business for an initial consideration of 717 million USD is still awaiting approval from the State Administration for Market Regulation's antitrust review.

Under U.S. Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, Dingdong Maicai has classified its China business as a discontinued operation, while its overseas business is classified as a continuing operation; related China business assets and liabilities are classified as assets and liabilities held for sale.

In other words, before the transaction is completed, the China business remains the main source of revenue and profit for Dingdong Maicai; however, from an accounting presentation and future structure perspective, this business has entered a divestiture process.

In the first quarter, Dingdong Maicai's China business revenue reached 5.753 billion yuan, up 5.9% year-on-year. The overall gross margin was 29.9%, flat with the same period last year; the fulfillment cost ratio decreased from 22.9% to 20.6% compared to the same period last year.

The company stated that the growth of the China business mainly came from an increase in monthly active users, higher order frequency leading to increased order volume, and improved site density and market penetration in the East China region following the opening of new front-end warehouses. However, the decline in CPI for major categories such as pork also partially offset the revenue growth rate.

This aligns with Dingdong Maicai's adjustment direction over the past few years.

The advantage of the front-end warehouse model lies in its proximity to consumers and faster delivery, making it suitable for high-frequency fresh product demand; however, the challenges include heavy costs for rent, labor, delivery, and waste.

Once order density is insufficient, revenue growth can easily be eroded by fulfillment costs. Over the past few years, Dingdong Maicai has shifted from nationwide expansion to regional focus, essentially rebalancing scale and efficiency.

East China is a core market that Dingdong Maicai has long focused on, with relatively mature user habits, supply chain organization, warehouse network density, and fulfillment efficiency.

This is one of the backgrounds for Meituan's acquisition of Dingdong Maicai's China business. For Meituan, the value of Dingdong Maicai is not just a fresh e-commerce brand, but also a front-end warehouse network and fresh supply chain capability that has been operating in the East China market for many years with a certain level of order density. If the transaction is completed, these assets are likely to be integrated into Meituan's instant retail system, enhancing its fresh product fulfillment capabilities.

The overseas business, although still small in scale but growing rapidly, has begun to become an important clue for external observers to track Dingdong Maicai's post-transaction direction.

In the first quarter, Dingdong Maicai's overseas business revenue grew 195.2% year-on-year to 139 million yuan, but the net loss also expanded 199.6% year-on-year to 71.4 million yuan, still in a phase of high growth and high investment.

From public information, Dingdong Maicai's overseas business roughly includes two categories: one is import supply chain, meaning bringing overseas products into the domestic market through a global direct procurement system; the other is channel expansion, selling ready-made meals, fresh products, refrigerated food, and other goods to overseas markets.

Previously, the company had chosen Saudi Arabia as its first overseas expansion destination, attempting to sell ready-made meals, fresh products, refrigerated food, and general merchandise to the local market. Essentially, it was replicating its domestic experience in product development, supply chain organization, and front-end warehouse operations overseas.

The China business awaits transfer, while the overseas business is still immature. Dingdong Maicai is still in a true transition period.
